backups.name: West Route (Rock Mountain Trail)
backups.season: Late May-October (south aspect melts out early)
gear: 3+ liters of water (no reliable sources on route)
Sun hat, sunscreen, sun shirt — the lower trail has almost no shade
Sturdy boots with good ankle support (loose rock underfoot)
Layers for wind and exposure on the ridge
Microspikes / light ice axe for early-season snow on north-facing terrain (Rock Lake basin, upper ridge)
hazards: No reliable water on route — carry 3+ liters, more in hot weather
Steep, fully exposed south-facing switchbacks with heat/sun exposure and no shade
Sharp drop-offs near the Schilling Creek crossing and along the summit ridge scramble
Loose rock and talus on the upper ridge and final scramble to the true summit
Lingering snowfields on north-facing terrain (Rock Lake basin, upper ridge) into early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms common July-August on this exposed ridge
Habituated mountain goats near the summit — keep distance, don't let them approach for salt
Signed artillery-range warning at mile 2.6 on Trail #1587 — stay on the established trail
backups.overview: Rock Mountain (6,800s ft) is the second-highest point on Nason Ridge, about 6.3 miles northeast of Stevens Pass and directly above US-2, in the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest. The standard trail (Rock Mountain Trail #1587) is one of the steepest maintained trails in the Stevens Pass area — a relentless, sun-exposed climb up a dry south-facing rib — earning the mountain a reputation as a 'workhorse' summit. It tops out at the site of a long-removed fire lookout, with expansive views to Glacier Peak, Mount Howard, Mount Mastiff, and the Monte Cristo group (Sloan, Pugh, Three Fingers), and is known for its wildflower meadows and resident mountain goats.
backups.beta: The West Route follows Trail #1587 from US-2 through a short stretch of forest and beneath power lines, leaves an old service road at about 0.5 mile, and begins a long, exposed switchbacking climb up Nason Ridge's flank (roughly 2,300 ft of gain in the first ~2 miles, 90+ switchbacks). Around 2-3 miles the grade eases as the trail contours into meadows near the Nason Ridge Trail junction (~6,000 ft); from there it continues past Rock Lake and a saddle near the Snowy Creek Trail junction, over a false summit, to the old lookout foundation and true summit.
backups.turnaround: The old lookout site along the ridge makes a reasonable lower turnaround/lunch spot if you don't want the full ridge walk to the true summit. Given the afternoon-thunderstorm risk on this exposed ridge, set and respect a firm turnaround time rather than pushing for the summit late in the day.
backups.face: South/southwest slope above Schilling Creek to the Nason Ridge crest, then the final ridge/summit block
backups.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
backups.descent: Same route (walk-off); no rappels or technical descent required.

waypoints.name: Rock Mountain Trailhead (US-2, MP 73)
waypoints.note: Signed USFS trailhead on the north side of US-2 near milepost 73 (~27 mi west of Leavenworth); no fee/permit and no water at the TH, so carry all you need — the trail stays dry for miles.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is a small dirt pullout on the north side of US 2 near milepost 73, about 27 miles west of Leavenworth, at roughly 2,675 feet. Look for the signed Rock Mountain Trail #1587 and the powerlines the trail climbs under; it is an easy pullout to drive past. There is no fee or permit and no facilities of any kind. There is also no water at the trailhead and essentially none above the creek low on the trail, so fill everything at the car.

waypoints.name: Decommissioned road bend / lookout sign
waypoints.note: Old service/powerline road bends sharply left at a Rock Mountain Lookout sign; trail narrows here and the real switchback climb begins.
waypoints.directions: The trail leaves the dirt lot and starts uphill immediately on what used to be a service road, passing beneath the powerlines. At about a third of a mile a signed bend marks where the route leaves the old roadbed and narrows to true single-track. Schilling Creek runs close to the tread just above here and is the only accessible water on the climb, so fill up: it drops away and there is essentially none above.

waypoints.name: Old artillery-range warning sign
waypoints.note: A weathered military impact-area warning sign along the switchbacks — a legacy of WWII-era training use of the ridge; stay on the tread, don't dig around old debris.
waypoints.directions: From the roadbed the trail settles into a relentless run of tight switchbacks, ninety-plus of them, up an open south and southwest-facing slope with no shade at all, which makes this a hot ascent and an early start worth the alarm. A ledgy switchback around 1 mile gives the first real view down-valley, and by roughly 2.1 miles and 5,000 ft the grade eases as the switchbacks give way to open hillside. The weathered sign appears shortly after; stay on the tread and leave any old debris where it lies.

waypoints.name: Nason Ridge Trail #1583 junction
waypoints.note: Rock Mountain Trail #1587 tops out at a saddle and meets Nason Ridge Trail; go left (north) for the summit, right drops toward a Rock Lake overlook (lake itself stays out of reach from this junction).
waypoints.directions: A little more easy climbing brings you into heather-carpeted subalpine meadows around 2.8 miles, and the trail tops out on the crest at the signed junction. This is the key navigational decision of the day: go left along the ridge for the summit, while the right-hand branch drops away toward a Rock Lake overlook.

waypoints.name: Lingering snowfield below the summit ridge
waypoints.note: A north-facing snow patch in the alpine meadows here can persist into fall and gets slick by afternoon; an ice axe or trekking poles help on firm snow.
waypoints.directions: Turn left and follow the crest. A north-facing snow patch sits in the meadows just up the ridge and can persist into fall, going slick through the afternoon and firm again in morning shade. An ice axe or at least trekking poles help on it, and microspikes are commonly worth carrying early season.

waypoints.name: Snowy Creek Trail alternate junction
waypoints.note: Secondary approach via Snowy Creek Trail #1531 joins the ridge crest here; ridge tread past this point is loose, jumbled talus — watch your footing.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the ridge crest to where the Snowy Creek Trail #1531 joins from the south; that is the alternate approach off Smithbrook Road, not your line. Past this junction the tread thins into more of a ridge scramble path over loose, jumbled talus, so watch your footing.

waypoints.name: Rock Mountain summit (old lookout site)
waypoints.note: Stone foundation of the former fire lookout marks the true summit; views take in Mount Howard, Mount Mastiff, Glacier Peak, and on clear days Baker and Rainier.
waypoints.directions: The path runs on over a false south summit. The short connecting ridge from there to the true summit is narrow and wants real care, and it can hold a cornice or residual snow into early summer. The stone foundation of the old lookout marks the top; you re-cross that connecting ridge first thing on the way down, and the loose switchbacks below are harder on knees and ankles descending than they were climbing.

what_to_bring: Map or GPS track — the final push to the true summit is an unmarked Class 2 scramble off the maintained trail
Northwest Forest Pass if starting from an alternate trailhead that requires one (not needed at the #1587 US-2 trailhead)
Bug spray for the lower forested switchbacks in early summer
Camera — summit views reach Glacier Peak, Mount Howard, Mount Mastiff, and the Monte Cristo peaks (Sloan, Pugh, Three Fingers)
pro_tips: Start at first light — the lower trail has zero shade and gets brutally hot by mid-morning in summer
The Snowy Creek approach (Trail #1531 via FR-6700/6705) is longer (9.8 mi) but only 3,250 ft of gain — a gentler grade than the direct #1587 grind, if you don't mind the brushy access road
Rock Lake, visible from the ridge saddle near the #1583 junction, is not reached by this route
Mountain goats are regularly seen on the upper mountain and can be habituated to hikers — keep your distance.
watch_out: The signed artillery-range warning at mile 2.6 — safe as long as you stay on the trail
No water past the trailhead — top off before you start
Start at dawn to beat the heat and afternoon thunderstorm risk
Mountain goats near the summit — give them room, don't feed or approach them
backups.best_season: South-facing exposure lets Trail #1587 melt out earlier than most Cascade routes at this elevation — often hikable by late June in light-snow years — but the north-facing Rock Lake basin and the upper ridge/summit scramble can hold snow into early July. Peak wildflowers (lupine, paintbrush, valerian, scarlet gilia) bloom mid-July through early August. Afternoon thunderstorms are common on this exposed ridge in July-August, so plan an early start. Fall (September-October) brings comfortable temperatures and golden larches along the ridge, but shorter days and the possibility of early snow.
backups.approach: From the Rock Mountain Trail #1587 pullout on US-2 (small dirt lot on the north side of the highway near the powerlines, no facilities), the trail launches immediately uphill on what was formerly a service road. At about 0.33 mile a signed junction marks where the route leaves the old roadbed, narrows to true single-track, and begins climbing alongside Schilling Creek — the creek runs close to the tread here but drops away and is not a reliable water source higher up, so top off early; there is essentially no accessible water for the rest of the climb. From here the trail settles into a long, relentless run of tight switchbacks (climbers count 90-plus) up an open, south/southwest-facing slope with zero shade, making this a notably hot ascent in summer. Around 1 mile a ledgy switchback opens the first real views down-valley. By roughly 2.1 miles (~5,000 ft) the grade eases as the switchbacks give way to more open hillside; at about 2.6 miles the trail passes an old (inactive) artillery-range warning sign, a quirky historical landmark, before entering heather-carpeted subalpine meadows around 2.8 miles. At roughly 3.2 miles and 6,000+ feet the trail tops out on the crest at a junction with the Nason Ridge Trail #1583 — this is the key navigational junction; go left (west) along the ridge. Around 3.7 miles the route passes the junction with the alternate Snowy Creek Trail #1531 approach (reached via Smithbrook Road #6700, a longer but more scenic drive-in), which joins from the south. Beyond this the tread thins into more of a ridge scramble path leading to a false (south) summit; use real caution on the short, narrow connecting ridge over to the true summit, which can hold a cornice or residual snow into early summer. The old lookout foundation and true summit (~6,850 ft) is reached around 3.95-4.0 miles one-way. Overall this is a Class 1-2 trail/scramble with no technical climbing when snow-free, but expect loose scree on sections of the switchbacks, essentially no shade or water above the creek crossing, and genuine route-finding/exposure caution on the false-summit-to-true-summit ridge, especially with snow present.
backups.descent_text: Descend by the same line you came up — Rock Mountain's West Route is an out-and-back scramble with no rappelling involved (0 rappels). From the true summit, re-cross the narrow, sometimes corniced connecting ridge back to the false (south) summit, then drop back onto the Rock Mountain Trail #1587 tread, passing the Snowy Creek Trail #1531 junction (~3.7 mi) and the Nason Ridge Trail #1583 junction (~3.2 mi) on your way back down into the meadows and then into the long switchback section. The loose, rocky switchbacks are noticeably harder on knees and ankles heading down than they were on the way up — trekking poles help a lot here. In early season, when snow lingers on the upper switchbacks and across the false-summit ridge, microspikes are commonly recommended for the descent since the slope faces southwest and can get soft and post-holey by midday, then firm and slick in morning/evening shade. Retrace back through the ~0.33-mile junction onto the old roadbed to the trailhead.
backups.bail: The Nason Ridge Trail (#1583) junction at roughly 3.2 miles is the last easy bail point before the exposed ridge walk and summit scramble; from there it's a straightforward reversal of the switchbacks back to the trailhead.

itinerary.cal: Best attempted late summer once snow clears near Rock Lake and the upper ridge; the lower switchbacks are hot and shadeless, so an early start matters more than season timing.

days.note: A single relentless day: roughly 90-99 switchbacks climb southeast-facing, largely shadeless slopes from the Hwy 2 trailhead up through Ponderosa forest into alpine meadows near Rock Lake, then a short jumbled-rock ridge walk to the summit. No camping, no technical gear — just an early start, steady pace, and plenty of water.
days.title: Car-to-car via Rock Lake / Trail #1587

schedule.label: Leave trailhead on Old Rd 667
schedule.detail: Start at first light to beat the heat on the exposed, shadeless lower switchbacks.

schedule.label: Break into alpine meadows
schedule.detail: Around 5,000 ft the forest opens into meadows with valley views; trail continues over jumbled rock in places.

schedule.label: Reach Rock Lake basin
schedule.detail: Junction area where the longer Snowy Creek approach joins; snowfields can linger here into early summer.

schedule.label: Summit ridge
schedule.detail: Careful footing on loose rock along the final ridge to the true summit.

schedule.label: Summit (6,852 ft)
schedule.detail: Aim to be off the exposed ridge before typical summer-afternoon thunderstorms build.

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Descend the same trail; total car-to-car time typically 7-9 hours depending on pace and conditions.

days.objective: Summit Rock Mountain (6,852 ft) and return same day

itinerary.totalNote: A long single day: ~8 miles round trip, 4,050 ft gain, typically 7-9 hours car-to-car with no camping required.

access.fees: None at the Rock Mountain Trailhead (#1587). $5 day-use or $30 annual pass (NW Forest Pass accepted) at some other Nason Ridge access points.
access.rules: Stay on the established trail at the signed artillery-range warning near mile 2.6. Trail #1587 is not recommended for stock or mountain bikes. Give mountain goats a wide berth — don't let them approach for salt or urine; haze them away if they linger near the trail or a rest stop.
access.permit: No permit required at the Rock Mountain Trailhead (#1587) off US-2. If starting instead from the Nason Ridge Trailhead at Kahler Glen (Lake Wenatchee side) or other developed Nason Ridge trailheads, a Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful pass is required.
access.closures: Check current Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest / Wenatchee River Ranger District alerts before you go — the district has had storm-damage road closures in recent years, and the brushy FR-6700/6705 access for the Snowy Creek approach is particularly susceptible to washouts and blowdown.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District
access.passRequired: None at the primary US-2 trailhead; Northwest Forest Pass required at some alternate trailheads (e.g., Kahler Glen/Nason Ridge Trailhead).

overnight_permit.where: Nason Ridge is national forest land outside any wilderness; a recreation pass may be needed at the trailheads.

road.name: US-2 roadside trailhead (Trail #1587) or Smith Brook Rd (FR-6700) → FR-6705 for the Snowy Creek approach
road.status: US-2 trailhead is reached via paved highway year-round (weather permitting); FR-6700 is decent gravel; FR-6705 is narrow and heavily brushed-in — passable but expect vehicle pinstriping, high clearance recommended.
road.driveNote: Trail #1587: from Leavenworth, US-2 west ~27 miles to a small pullout on the north side near milepost 73, 0.4 mi east of the WSDOT buildings. Snowy Creek: from US-2 about 4 miles east of Stevens Pass, turn onto Smith Brook Road/FR-6700, go 6.0 miles, turn right onto FR-6705, go 3.6 miles to the trailhead.
road.seasonalGate: Not gated, but FR-6705 may be brushed-in or storm-damaged early in the season; check current FS road status before driving it.

climate.typical: East-Cascades rain-shadow climate: dry, sunny, often hot summers with little to no shade on the lower switchbacks, and cold, snowy winters. Afternoon thunderstorms build regularly in July-August.

bySeason.fall: Comfortable hiking temperatures and golden larches along the ridge; days shorten quickly and the first snow can arrive by mid-to-late October.
bySeason.spring: Lower south-facing switchbacks can be snow-free by late June in light-snow years, but expect lingering snow and potential postholing above the Rock Lake saddle and on the summit ridge into early July.
bySeason.summer: Hot and dry on the exposed lower trail with little to no shade; carry more water than you think, as there are no reliable sources. Afternoon thunderstorms build on most days in July-August.
bySeason.winter: Snowbound and avalanche-prone terrain; not a winter hiking objective.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Stevens Pass zone for general mountain weather/avalanche context (winter/spring); no dedicated NWAC summer product — check Okanogan-Wenatchee NF / Wenatchee River Ranger District alerts for trail conditions and fire restrictions in summer.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable to nonexistent along this stretch of US-2 and on the ridge itself; don't count on a signal until you're back near the Stevens Pass summit or in Leavenworth/Coles Corner.
emergency.rangerStation: Wenatchee River Ranger District, 600 Sherbourne St, Leavenworth, WA 98826 — (509) 548-2550 (Mon/Tue/Thu/Fri 9am-12pm & 1-3:30pm; closed Wed & federal holidays)
emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Medical Center, 817 Commercial St, Leavenworth, WA — critical-access hospital roughly 27 miles / ~40 min via US-2. Central Washington Hospital in Wenatchee (full trauma services) is about 48 miles away.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Chelan County Sheriff's Office non-emergency (509) 667-6845; dial 911 for emergencies. Chelan County Sheriff coordinates backcountry search and rescue in this area.

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekend mornings July-September during wildflower bloom; early starts (before ~8am) reported as having the trail to yourself
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Low-to-moderate; trailhead pullout is small (room for only a handful of cars), which naturally caps volume — likely a few dozen parties over a season, not a mega-popular trade route

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong aerobic fitness required — 8 mi round trip with ~4,050 ft gain at an average grade over 18%, with steep switchbacks concentrated early in the hike
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day-hiking load, roughly 15-25 lb (water, layers, navigation, snow gear if early season)

partner_requirements.approachTime: Full day; 5-7 hours round trip is typical, longer if snow lingers or party is less conditioned
requiredSkills: Sustained steep trail hiking / pacing on relentless switchbacks
Basic Class 2 scrambling and route-finding along the summit ridge
Snow travel / self-arrest awareness and route-finding if climbing early season while snow lingers on upper switchbacks
Heat management — trail is exposed and reported as hot with little shade
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate hiker comfortable with sustained steep grades and basic Class 2 off-trail/ridge scrambling near the summit; not a beginner-friendly trail due to relentless switchbacks

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September as the leading edge of the window; conditions remain climbable into October

July.reason: Season opens as snow melts out; lingering snow on the trail early in the month, and wildflower bloom is beginning

August.reason: Peak wildflower meadows and most reliable dry, snow-free footing on the switchbacks

October.reason: Early snow/ice possible at elevation and on the exposed switchbacks; shorter daylight window for the full 8-mile round trip

September.reason: Stable dry weather, fall colors, fewer bugs; one of the best months for the steep exposed trail

weather.typical: Warm, dry east-slope Cascades summer conditions; the trail is steep and hot with little shade on the switchbacks
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are possible in July-August in the Cascades; check forecast before committing to the exposed upper trail

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Trail itself is steep with loose footing (switchbacks, loose rock); the summit ridge walk is Class 2 walking terrain with some exposure but not technical. Fall consequence is low-to-moderate on dry trail, elevated on the upper switchbacks if lingering early-season snow or ice is present

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route; climbed mid-July through October, after the NWAC-forecasted avalanche season for the nearest zone (Stevens Pass) has ended

gaps: Summit elevation varies notably by source (6,808-6,860 ft depending on DEM/topo used) — treat 6,856 ft as approximate rather than surveyed
No confirmed first-ascent history; the mountain's name is attributed to USGS surveyor Albert H. Sylvester but no FA date/party is documented in available sources
No aggregated recent trip-report conditions consensus available beyond general seasonal guidance

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Rock Mountain Trail #1587 pullout on US-2 (small dirt lot on the north side of the highway near the powerlines, no facilities), the trail launches immediately uphill on what was formerly a service road.

backups.rope_note: Class 2 trail-based route via maintained Rock Mountain Trail #1587 (USFS) off US-2; no technical rock or rope gear needed.
backups.corrections: Confirmed via USFS trailhead page; maintained trail to near-summit scrambling only.

approach_variants.name: Trail #1587 from US-2 to the Nason Ridge crest
approach_variants.notes: One of the steepest maintained trails near Stevens Pass, and it starts working immediately. From the dirt pullout on the north side of the highway the tread climbs on an old service road beneath powerlines, leaves the roadbed at a signed bend about a third of a mile up, and then runs into ninety-odd tight switchbacks on an open south-facing slope with no shade at all. Schilling Creek near the bottom is the only accessible water on the climb and it drops away quickly, so fill everything at the car and carry three litres or more. The grade eases into heather meadows around 2.8 miles and the tread tops out on the crest at about 6,000 ft. An alternate approach comes up the Snowy Creek trail from the Smithbrook road and joins the ridge higher.
approach_variants.season: Late June to October; snow lingers
hazards: No reliable water on route above the creek low down
Fully exposed south-facing switchbacks with real heat and sun load
Loose rock and jumbled talus on the upper ridge
A north-facing snow patch below the summit ridge can persist into fall and goes slick by afternoon
A cornice or residual snow on the narrow connecting ridge into early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms on a wholly exposed crest
Habituated mountain goats near the summit — keep your distance
approach_variants.baseFinding: Two signed junctions bracket the start of the scrambling and neither is the base by itself. The first is where the trail tops out on the crest at roughly 6,000 ft and meets the Nason Ridge trail; turn left along the ridge here, since the right-hand branch drops away toward a lake overlook. The second, about half a mile on, is where the Snowy Creek trail joins from the south — that is the alternate approach, not your line, and past it the constructed tread stops being tread and thins into a path over loose jumbled talus. That change underfoot is the base. From there the crest runs over a false south summit first; it carries no structure on it. The true summit beyond is identified by the stone foundation of the old fire lookout, and the short connecting ridge between the two is narrow enough to want care and can hold a cornice or old snow into early summer. If you are standing on a high point with nothing built on it and the ridge carries on, keep going.

climbing_route.label: Ridge scramble path to the false (south) summit
climbing_route.notes: Past the Snowy Creek Trail #1531 junction the tread thins into more of a ridge scramble path leading to a false (south) summit. No technical climbing when snow-free, but expect loose scree on sections of the switchbacks and essentially no shade or water above the creek crossing.

climbing_route.label: Connecting ridge to the true summit (~6,850 ft)
climbing_route.notes: Use real caution on the short, narrow connecting ridge over to the true summit, which can hold a cornice or residual snow into early summer; genuine route-finding/exposure caution on the false-summit-to-true-summit ridge, especially with snow present. The old lookout foundation and true summit (~6,850 ft) is reached around 3.95-4.0 miles one-way.

bivy.name: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
bivy.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. The season runs roughly May through mid-October. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed campgrounds through the operating season, and Nason Creek itself alongside. This is the one place where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
bivy.capacity: Nason Creek is the closest and largest, laid out over four loops on both sides of the highway near the southeastern end of Lake Wenatchee, taking vehicles up to about thirty-five feet. Roughly sixty percent of sites are reservable in advance and the remainder are first come, first served. The state park campgrounds around the lake add substantially more capacity, and there are further national forest campgrounds spread along the highway corridor.

bivy.name: Rock Lake
bivy.notes: The camp for Rock Mountain and the western anchor of the whole crest. The Rock Mountain trail leaves US 2 at about 2,650 feet and is relentless — roughly 3,400 feet in four miles of endless switchbacks on a hot, open, south-facing slope with no water and very little shade, which is the single most quoted complaint about this peak. The lake sits in a basin below the summit ridge, so a party that has ground up the trail can drop packs, camp, and take the northeast ridge and the summit unencumbered. Most people do Rock Mountain in a day; camping here is what you do when the heat has beaten you, when you are starting the Nason Ridge traverse rather than finishing it, or when you want the summit at first light. The alternative approach by the Snowy Creek trail from the forest road on the north side starts higher and climbs less, and it is the kinder line in warm weather, though the road is brushy. Snow lingers on the upper slopes into early summer and the basin holds it later than the trail below. West of the lake, the crest trail toward Crescent Lake has badly eroded steep sidehill sections with little tread left, and that stretch is the crux of moving along this ridge with a pack.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is the first water of any kind on the Rock Mountain trail — the entire climb from the highway is dry. It holds all season. Treat it, because the shoreline is well used and the basin is small. Fill here for everything you intend to do on the crest, since the next dependable source westward or eastward is Crescent Lake, and the ridge between the two carries nothing.
bivy.permit: None. Nason Ridge sits outside the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery anywhere. The Rock Mountain trailhead has very limited parking, though no fee is charged there and the Merritt Lake end requires no pass either; of the trailheads serving this crest only Nason Ridge is a fee site, at $5 a day or $30 a year. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which covers this camp and every other high site here, and summer burn bans are routine on this dry east-side ground.
bivy.capacity: Several pleasant established sites around the lake, enough for two or three parties; small and it feels small, with no facilities
